trajectory_summary: This is a short qualification call that surfaced a hard disqualifier almost immediately: the home already has a broken, SolarCity-installed system, which Ion cannot service. The rep handled the discovery cleanly — verified via Google Maps, asked the right clarifying questions, and correctly declined to attempt a repair sale — but the call ends with no appointment and no path forward once the customer's actual need (fixing an existing broken system) turned out to be outside Ion's offerings.
outcome_dispute: v1 tag is 'unknown' — this call should be tagged 'dq', not booked/tentative/callback. The customer has an existing, non-working solar system installed by SolarCity (a named hard-DQ competitor per dq_rules.sunrun_existing/pink_solar_existing analog and orphaned_flow.existing_system_broken), and the call ends with the customer declining further engagement ('No. Thank you.') with no next step captured.

observed_outcome.reasoning: Customer has an existing solar system installed by SolarCity that is not working; Ion cannot service or repair third-party systems, and the customer declined the narrower battery/panel offer, ending the call with no appointment set.

bill_anchor_audit.reasoning: The call never reached bill collection — it was diverted into orphaned-system triage almost immediately after the address was confirmed, and ended in a hard DQ before any bill question was asked.

interest_reason_audit.reason_quote: No. It's just the panel is not working now.
interest_reason_audit.use_quote: to get those back going again, you'd have to contact SolarCity, and they they would be able to help you with that.
interest_reason_audit.reasoning: The rep asked about panels vs. battery, and when the customer revealed the actual reason (broken panels), the rep used that information immediately to correctly route the customer to the original installer and identify the DQ, rather than filing it and moving on.

primary_coaching_focus.topic: closing a hard-DQ call without a door-leave
primary_coaching_focus.why: The DQ itself was handled correctly, but the call ends flatly with no attempt to keep the lead warm (callback offer, note for a future battery/panel need) — a low-cost addition that could matter if this customer's situation changes.

key_moments.quote: on Google Maps. It looks like you have solar panels.
key_moments.stewart_read: The rep discovers via satellite imagery — not via the standard verify flow — that this is an orphaned-system call rather than a new-install lead. He adapts appropriately, but this is exactly the scenario the orphaned_flow schema section exists for, and the rep runs it from memory rather than a visibly structured checklist.

key_moments.quote: Were you was it additional panels or was it a backup battery?
key_moments.stewart_read: The rep asks a binary qualifying question but the underlying situation (non-working panels) hasn't surfaced yet — this is a reasonable verify-stage question, not a major miss, but it shows the rep hadn't yet probed why the customer reached out, which would have surfaced the broken-system issue one turn earlier.

Customer names the original installer (heard by rep as SolarCity). The rep uses this correctly to identify the hard-DQ condition, but never asks anything further about the original install (when installed, system size, why it failed) that could have been useful context.

key_moments.quote: But I so I I'm not able to help get those working again. But if you were wanting to get, like, a backup battery or additional panels, I can help you with getting that.
key_moments.stewart_read: The rep correctly offers the two things Ion could still sell (battery, additional panels) into this DQ situation. This is the right instinct — reframing a hard DQ into a narrower cross-sell attempt — even though the customer ultimately declines.
